Border Empires UI Teardown
Border Empires · HUD overhaul · draft 4 · 25 Oct 2026

UI Teardown

Twenty reference screens from six 4X games, broken into reusable patterns. Each pattern gets a verdict for Border Empires: keep adapt discard later. The verdicts feed a desktop layout, two dedicated screens (town and battle), and a mobile version.

Changes since draft 1
  • Manpower moves out of the top bar into an orb in the bottom right, with an empty state that says what you can still do. The orb shows manpower only. Things waiting on you sit at the top of the tracker.
  • The minimap moves to the bottom left.
  • The crest and destinations become bubbles under the resource bar.
  • Open town ▸ (or a double-click) opens a town screen with its own UI. The tracker, minimap, rivals, action bar and advisor are hidden there. The orb stays, because building costs manpower.
  • New battle screen: you on the left, the other side on the right, expected outcome in the bottom middle.
  • Outliner removed. The tracker covers what matters.
  • The clock is now Season day 9. A season has no fixed length: it ends when someone holds a victory path for 24 hours, so there's no "days left" to show.
  • Relations score moved from later to keep. AI attitude already exists as named modifiers on the trade screen.
  • Review fixes (draft 4): frontier attacks skip the battle screen. Towns open via Open town ▸. The tile panel sits above the action bar. The tracker is capped. The orb stays on the town screen. Ranks shows only the data the client gets. Coin everywhere. Shortcuts no longer clash. Mobile tabs are fixed. A renderer-parity list is added.
How we work through this
  1. Inventory
    List every panel the client has today.
  2. Teardown
    Break references into patterns and give each a verdict.
  3. Blueprint
    Map, town and battle layouts. Every current panel gets a home.
  4. Visual direction
    One frame style, type scale and icon grammar.
  5. Hi-fi mock
    Desktop HUD in Storybook over a real map capture.
  6. Mobile
    Same information, laid out for thumbs.
  7. Migrate
    New shell behind a flag, panels moved one at a time.

The lens: what makes Border Empires different

All six references are turn-based (Stellaris is pausable real-time) and five of them have units. Border Empires has neither, so a lot of their chrome has nothing to attach to here. These are the filters every pattern went through.

Real-time, persistentNo End Turn. The core loop says "every visit is a turn", so the HUD should answer "what can I do right now, and when should I come back".
No unitsNo unit cards or stacks. Military is manpower and borders. A battle is two tiles and two sets of modifiers, resolved in 15 seconds.
Manpower is the gateEvery physical action costs MP, so it gets its own orb, the way AoW4 gives the turn its own orb.
Slots, not stockpilesFood, Titanium, Crystal and Umbrite are slot capacity. They read as used / total, never as a growing number with a +rate.
Borders are the pictureThe map's main visual is border colour and integrity. The HUD frames the map and stays off it.
Phones and the 2D map are first-classMany players are on mobile, and the 2D renderer is the fallback for weak devices. Nothing in the HUD can depend on 3D.

Game by game

What each game does best, what we take from it, and what we leave.

Age of Wonders 4

The richest information design of the set. Every number can be opened to see where it comes from.

  • keepTooltips that break a number down into named modifiers with values. Integrity, manpower and Coin income should all work like this.
  • keepGlowing, owner-coloured borders that stay readable on busy terrain. This is the closest reference to our map.
  • keepThe city screen (Halheim): a left column with the city's identity and yields, a build list next to it, and the map zoomed on the city. ◁ ▷ arrows step through your cities. This is the model for our town screen.
  • keepEmpire Relations with modifiers. Our AI attitude (Furious to Friendly) is already a sum of named modifiers, so it can use this tooltip as is.
  • adaptThe orb in the bottom right becomes the manpower orb. The "orders required" count moves into the tracker, so the orb shows only manpower.
  • adaptThe medallion with a row of round buttons beside it becomes the House crest and five destination bubbles under the resource bar.
  • adaptThe diplomacy face-off (you on the left, them on the right, offers in the middle). This is also the layout for our battle screen.
  • discardGold filigree on every frame, and a top bar packed with 14 small icons.

Age of Wonders: Planetfall

Clean sci-fi chrome, with a tech tree you can read across a room.

  • keepThe tech tree laid out as tier columns and themed lanes, with small icons of what each tech unlocks on its node. This is our Manifest "Tree view".
  • adaptAn advisor character, as short cards that come and go rather than modals. Who the voice is needs a lore check. The Sable Recollections' Duke is the obvious candidate, but "Duke" is also the title the season winner earns, and an advisor called the Duke would blur that.
  • discardThe welcome modal that covers the map on first load. Onboarding should happen on the map.

Endless Legend 2

Building is the core verb, and it shows you the result before you commit.

  • keepA placement preview showing yield changes on the tile before you confirm. We already have a placement overlay. It needs the numbers.
  • keepA structure card with artwork, the effect, prerequisites and cost in one consistent order. One template for every structure.
  • keepThe battle framing: attacker panel on one side, defender on the other, attack preview along the bottom. We drop the tactical part (units, rounds, hex moves) and keep the framing for our battle screen.
  • adaptA quest tracker in the top-left corner, merged with Civ6's tracker into ours.
  • discardTactical battle controls (rounds, auto/manual, unit stats). Our fights resolve on the server in 15 seconds.

Civilization VII

The most restrained of the set. Each choice tells you its net effect.

  • keepA net-effect pill on every choice card (+16 ♪ −8 ☺), computed for your empire. AFC upgrades and Manifests should state their result for you, not only a rule.
  • discard"Current research" with three choices. Every Manifest costs the same and arrives at once, so a pick-three would hide the tree for no reason. The tree is the default view.
  • keepA compact tile tooltip: terrain, yields, owner, improvement.
  • keepProduction rows with icon, yield and time. This is the model for the town screen's build list.
  • laterThe radial menu. A long-press ring could work on mobile.

Civilization VI

The tracker that always tells you what's in progress.

  • keepA world tracker in the top-left. Ours lists what needs you, your muster flags, builds and battles in progress, and the victory race. Manifests have no timer, so there's no research row. It replaces the floating capture card.
  • keepLenses (map overlays you toggle). We have resource and integrity overlays already. They get one switcher on the minimap frame.
  • discardYield icons on every tile by default.

Stellaris

The only real-time reference.

  • discardThe Outliner. In Stellaris it tracks fleets and ships you have to find again. We have no units, and your towns are already visible on the map. The tracker covers everything with a timer.
  • adaptA date readout in the corner becomes the season clock.
  • discardPause and speed controls, tiny grey text, and a 13-resource strip.

How the action bar works

It's today's tile menu moved to one fixed place. Select a tile and the bar shows only what you can do on that tile. The main action is a big button with its manpower cost. Everything else (the full build list, Aether abilities, diplomacy) sits behind ⋯. You never see Expand, Garrison, Build and Attack together. The first draft drew them that way to show all four, and that was misleading.

Each main action gets a single-key shortcut on desktop (E, G, B, A). On mobile the bar sits at the bottom of the tile sheet.

Muster flags

Today your flags are listed inside the manpower panel ("Active muster flags"), and each flag has a % badge on the map. The new HUD puts them where you'll see them, in three places:

Click a flag to centre and select it · its actions open on the action bar
  • In the tracker, a Flags group. One row per flag: name, mode (Hold, Advance, March), how full it is against its cap, and what it's doing right now. That covers fighting at a tile, marching with tiles taken, clearing an area, waiting for its next action, or holding. All of this is already on the flag's state.
  • Problems go to Needs you. These are states where a flag is stuck: insufficient manpower, no target in range, target it can't fund, and under siege. Each one says what's wrong in plain words and links to the flag.
  • On the orb. The hover shows manpower staged in flags ("180 in 3 flags"), because flags draw from the same pool. Players asking "where did my manpower go?" get the answer in the right place.
  • On the map, the existing % badges stay as they are in both renderers, with the siege ring and guarding soldiers.

When it runs out

The orb drains and dims, and clicking it says one of two things

Refill with a Shard (if you hold one), shown first. See below.

You can still act: "No manpower until 21:40. You can still commission a Manifest (170 Coin) and upgrade Halveth (Coin)." Each item is a button that takes you there. These are the things that cost Coin or Shard instead of manpower.

Nothing left to do: "You're done for now. Manpower refills at 21:40 (in 2h 14m)." It also offers a reminder if we add notifications.

It also shows how to raise the cap: hold more towns, grow town tiers, and the Ancillary Depot. Those are the sources the economy already has.

in the game · Shard Mobilization

Donate Shard: +308 manpower. This is the first button on the empty-state panel, above the two messages. Donating 1 Shard to the Court refills manpower to the cap at once, never above it. Today the card sits deep inside the manpower panel. The orb brings it forward at the moment you need it.

The button uses the server's own reasons when it's unavailable: no Shard held ("You hold 0"), manpower already full, or regen frozen by your Titanium Levy. The Shard chip's tooltip also says what Shards are for (Monumental parts and Mobilization), so the two places agree.

Town screen

Selecting your town shows its tile panel like any tile, so quick actions (a muster flag, an ability) stay one click away. Open town ▸, a double-click or Enter then zooms the map onto it and swaps the HUD. The resource bar and the manpower orb stay, because builds spend Coin, slots and manpower. Everything else steps aside: tracker, minimap, rivals, action bar, advisor. Modelled on AoW4's city screen.

Battle screen

You are always on the left, whether you're attacking or defending, and the side is labelled with a verb. Your eye learns where "mine" is once, as in AoW4's diplomacy screen. The data is already there: the server's attack preview sends a win chance plus a named breakdown for each side (base, infrastructure modifiers, battle modifiers, effective strength).

When does it open?

Not when you click an enemy tile. Clicking one selects it like any other tile: the tile panel shows who owns it, and the action bar shows Attack (with the win chance on the button), Diplomacy, and the rest behind ⋯. The battle screen only opens once you've chosen to attack, so its button is Confirm attack, not Launch.

Fights are short and some are automatic. A muster flag on Advance can run three at once. A full screen for every fight would get in the way, so it opens in three cases:

  • After you press Attack on garrisoned land, as the confirm step where you pick effort. Attacking plain frontier is a guaranteed capture with no roll, so it fires straight away with no screen, which keeps the most common attack at one click. Effort only appears where it changes the odds. A setting ("Skip attack confirm") or Alt+click reuses your last effort for players taking many tiles in a row. Shift is already box select.
  • From the tracker, by clicking a battle in progress. It shows the live countdown and then the result.
  • When you're attacked and it matters: a town, a dock or your AFC. A toast says "Halveth under attack · View". Defending isn't a spectator screen. The attacker's launch tile isn't locked by the fight, so the screen offers Counter-attack their launch tile with its own odds, plus Raise a flag here.

Fights started by flags only go to the tracker.

March is an order, not a battle, and not a waypoint. It's an attack in a direction: the flag pushes toward the target, taking frontier and garrisoned enemy tiles and neutral land on the way, and re-aims every tick as the map changes. There's no fixed path, so a single win chance wouldn't mean much. March mode shows the direction and what stands in it:

  • A heading on the map: an arrow from the flag to the target, with the tiles in its way tinted by type: neutral, enemy frontier, garrisoned enemy, fogged.
  • What's in the way, roughly: "About 11 tiles · 4 neutral · 3 enemy frontier · 4 garrisoned · 2 fogged". It's labelled an estimate, because the push re-aims.
  • The strongest position in the way, by name: "Strongest: Halveth (fort town) · 48%". That's where the push is most likely to stall.
  • Manpower the flag commits, since every fight costs its commitment, win or lose.

The button reads Send march. The tracker shows "Marching on Halveth · 4 tiles taken". Each fight on the way appears as it happens and opens the live battle screen.

The client can estimate the tiles in the way from what it can see. The strongest-position odds need a preview from the server for a tile that isn't next to your land, which doesn't exist today.

Destination screens: Manifest, AFC upgrades, Diplomacy, Ranks, Chronicle

Manifest, AFC upgrades, Diplomacy and Ranks are full screens and share one frame. Chronicle is a drawer over the live map instead, because its rows point at places on the map (see below).

  • The resource bar and the bubble row stay, with the open screen's bubble lit. Click another bubble to switch, or Esc to go back to the map.
  • The map stays behind, darkened and slightly blurred. You never fully leave the world.
  • The map HUD (tracker, minimap, rivals, action bar, orb, advisor) is hidden, as on the town screen.
  • Each screen has a list on the left and the detail on the right, except Manifest and AFC upgrades, which are a tree and a board.

Manifest and AFC upgrades: how the two connect

These two screens form one progression, so they should explain each other.

  • Manifest is the tech tree: 41 Manifests in 4 lanes (Economy, Manpower, War, Aether) across 5 tiers. You commission one with Coin and it arrives at once. There's no research timer and no points. Every Manifest costs the same at any moment, and each one you buy raises the price of the rest (10, 40, 70, 100, 130, 170 …). So the decision is what it unlocks, never which one is cheaper. Prerequisites gate the tree.
  • AFC upgrades are 30 free, permanent choices: 6 paths × 5 tiers, with one pick per tier, filled in order. The highest Manifest tier you own sets how far you can go. Buying a tier V Manifest early "banks" the picks below it. Installing needs an active AFC that you own.
  • So the loop is: commission a Manifest → it may open your next AFC pick → choose one of six. The Manifest tier headers show this link.

Manifest

Laid out like a Civ tech tree: each Manifest is a card with art on the left, its name bar coloured by state, and a row of icons for everything it unlocks. You can read what a Manifest gives you without opening it, and hovering an icon shows that structure or ability's card. The tree sits on a see-through panel over the live map, so it feels like part of the world rather than a separate menu.

Ranks · the race for the Duke's seat

The season is a race along five victory paths. Whoever holds any path's threshold for 24 hours wins a Planet of their own and the title of Duke. So the screen is drawn as the race: five tracks with empire crests moving along them toward the win line, rather than a table with progress bars. You can see who's ahead on what, how close you are, and whether anyone is holding, before reading a single number. The plain standings move to the side.

~Standings keep the plain ranking with a trend line, for players who just want the table.

The thresholds and the 24-hour hold come from the season rules, and the client already receives the leader and hold time live. The positions on the tracks are example values. One catch: progress arrives as text labels ("31% of towns"), so placing crests needs either a numeric share added to the victory payload (a small protocol change) or parsing the labels. The first is safer. On mobile, the tracks stack full-width and the side column moves below them.

Chronicle · a drawer over the live map

Almost every Chronicle entry happened somewhere: a tile taken, a town grown, a shard site landing. So the map stays live and the timeline slides in from the left, where the tracker and minimap usually sit. Clicking a row flies the camera there and marks the tile. The drawer stays open, so you can step down the list and watch each event on the map. You can also click the map as normal, so "Ashford took (31,8)" leads straight to Attack on the action bar.

The clock

"Day 9 · 12d left" was wrong. A season has no maximum length. SEASON_LENGTH_DAYS = 30 is declared in config.ts but nothing reads it. A season ends when someone holds a victory path for 24 hours, so the clock counts up, and the timer that matters is the hold.

Recommended

Season day 9

The age of the world. Everyone shares it, and it tells you where you are in the arc (opening, build-up, war, victory race). Next to it goes the timer that actually matters: "Ashford holding Towns · 14h to win". Hovering shows all victory paths.

Empire age · 6 days

Personal, but it says little about what to do next, and it's confusing after a respawn. Better as a line on your profile.

Next manpower refill

The most useful timer for coming back, but it already lives on the orb.

Making resources look clickable

Today the chips look like labels. I'd keep them as chips and fix the affordance in four ways:

Coin 1,240 +38/hFood 4/6Ti 2/2Integrity 82%

Hover one. "Food" shows the hover state and "Ti" shows a warning state.

  • Every chip is a framed button with hover (gold edge, slight lift), pressed and focus states, and a pointer cursor.
  • The tooltip appears on hover with no delay and ends with "Click for full breakdown". That line teaches the click.
  • A chip with a problem gets a dot: a full slot, a dormant structure, integrity dropping. That gives people a reason to click.
  • On mobile the whole bar is one target. Tapping it opens a Treasury sheet with every resource and its breakdown, instead of seven tiny tap targets.

Visual direction

Most of the AAA feel comes from consistency, not ornament. Three ways to dress the layout:

Recommended

Imperial gilt, restrained

Continues the current Cinzel/Spectral and gold-on-ink look, with gold kept for frames, the orb and key numbers.

Option

Frontier instrument

Teal sci-fi chrome in the style of Planetfall. Means rebranding away from the current look.

Option

Brass and slate

Industrial, and goes with the steampunk icon set. A bigger step from today.

Rules that hold whichever direction we pick

  • One frame style used by every panel. No one-off cards.
  • Every number has a tooltip, and every tooltip says where the number comes from.
  • Three typefaces with fixed jobs: Cinzel for titles, Spectral for text, Space Mono for numbers.
  • One icon set at one stroke weight.
  • Panels slide in from the edge they're docked to. Modals only for decisions that can't be undone.
  • Every control has hover, pressed, disabled and focused states.
  • State is never colour alone: every state also has an icon or shape (✓, lock, hourglass ring, warning dot). Red, amber and green are kept for status, so a player who picks a red empire colour never reads as "hostile" or "holding".
  • The currency is called Coin everywhere, as in the lore and Diplomacy.

Still open

1. Battle screen triggers. Do the three cases above match what you had in mind, or should every fight you're in be able to open it?

2. Visual direction. Restrained gilt (recommended), frontier instrument, or brass and slate?

3. Victory data. Add a numeric share per path to the victory payload so Ranks can place crests, or parse today's text labels?

4. Opening your town. Open town ▸ plus double-click (proposed), or open straight away on a single click as before?

5. Advisor voice. Which character, given that "Duke" is also the prize title?

Next, once these are settled: hi-fi mocks of the map, town and battle screens in packages/storybook over a real map capture.
